title: Decode Ways
statement: A string of digits stands for a message. Digits 1 to 26 map to the letters A to Z, so "1" is A and "26" is Z. A digit string can often be cut into letters in several ways. Count how many different readings the whole string has. A leading zero never forms a letter.

output.label: dp[i] = ways to read the first i digits

idea.sentence: dp[i] counts the readings of the first i digits, and it is the sum of two cells behind it: dp[i-1] if the last digit alone is a letter, plus dp[i-2] if the last two digits make 10 to 26.

jargon.plain: Solve a big question by filling a table of smaller answers, each built from cells you already filled.
The first i characters of the string. dp[i] is about the prefix of length i.

watch.inputHint: One argument: a string of digits, e.g. "226"

vars.meaning: number of digits in the string

compare.bruteLabel: Try every way to cut the string
compare.optimalLabel: Fill one table cell per digit
compare.unit: readings visited (rough; the brute shape is exponential, 2n is the closest curve)

rows.name: Brute force recursion
rows.note: Each digit can start a one-digit or two-digit letter, and the same suffix is solved again and again.

rows.name: dp table
rows.note: One cell per prefix, each built from two earlier cells in constant time.

rows.name: Two rolling variables
rows.note: Only dp[i-1] and dp[i-2] are ever read, so keep just those two numbers.

fast.takeaway: The count for a prefix only depends on the two shorter prefixes before it, so one left-to-right pass fills the whole table.

stages.title: Base cell
stages.note: dp has n + 1 cells. dp[0] = 1 for the empty prefix, which gives later cells something to add.

stages.title: Last digit alone
stages.note: If the last digit is not 0, it is a letter by itself. Copy dp[i-1].

stages.title: Last two digits
stages.note: If the last two digits read 10 to 26, they are one letter. Add dp[i-2].

stages.title: Answer
stages.note: The whole string is the prefix of length n, so the answer is dp[n].

edges.title: Leading zero
edges.why: A zero cannot start a letter. "6" alone is fine but "06" is not 6, so nothing reads the string.

edges.title: Zero that must pair
edges.why: The 0 cannot stand alone, so only the pair 10 works. dp[2] gets dp[0] and nothing from dp[1].

edges.title: Pair too large
edges.why: 27 is over 26, so only 2-7 reads. The pair step adds nothing.

edges.title: Two zeros in a row
edges.why: The second 0 has no valid partner: 00 is not a letter and 0 alone is not one.

gotchas.text: Make the table n + 1 long. Index i means the first i digits, so dp[0] is the empty prefix and the answer is dp[n]. A table of length n shifts every index by one.
Check the pair as a number from 10 to 26, not just less than 27. "06" is the number 6, but it is not a valid pair because of its leading zero.
Compare digit characters, not numbers: s[i - 1] !== '0'. Writing s[i - 1] !== 0 is always true because a string never equals the number 0.
Indexing a string gives a byte, not a number. Subtract '0' to get the digit value. This is safe for digits, but would split non-ASCII text in the middle of a character.

recap.key: dp[i] = readings of the first i digits = (dp[i-1] if the last digit is not 0) + (dp[i-2] if the last two digits are 10 to 26).
recap.complexity: Time O(n). Space O(n), or O(1) with two variables.
moves: Make dp of length n + 1, with dp[0] = 1
For each i, add dp[i-1] when s[i-1] is not 0
Add dp[i-2] when the last two digits are 10 to 26
